newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ministerial envoy sent to Zaire, Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: French ministerial envoy sent to Zaire, Rwanda.

text.p: France on Sunday sent cabinet member Xavier Emmanuelli to Rwanda and Zaire to evaluate the situation on the ground ahead of a Canadian-led multinational mission to the region to aid refugees.

The goal of the trip by Emmanuelli, secretary of state for emergency humanitarian action, was "to evaluate the situation in the zone and to show France's solidarity with the humanitarian groups and non-governmental organisations which are working there," an aide to the minister told Reuters.
But French officials were silent on whether Paris was re-evaluating the mission due to the return to Rwanda in recent days of more than 200,000 refugees previously stranded in eastern Zaire.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the United States was consulting allies with an eye to modifying the plan.
But U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said a multinational force was still needed in troubled eastern Zaire.

Countries planning to contribute troops to the mission were due to meet in Stuttgart on Wednesday to review the force's size and mandate following the refugees' return, a U.S. military official in Germany said.
Asked whether the mission might be revised, a French official referred a reporter to a Foreign Ministry statement issued on Saturday.
The statement said that France was pleased by the refugees' return and that the aid mission might be completed before the March 31 expiration of its United Nations mandate.
Emmanuelli, who arrived in Kigali on Sunday afternoon, would remain in the region until Tuesday, travelling to the Zaire capital Kinshasa before returning to Paris.
The aide denied a radio report that Rwanda had initially denied him permission to land in Kigali.

Rwanda's predominantly Tutsi government accuses France of being partisan after it sent troops to Rwanda in 1994 to help stop Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus. It charges that Paris used the intervention to help protect Hutus responsible for instigating the mass killings.

Following Friday's U.N. approval of the multinational peace force, to be led by Canada, France said it was planning to deploy its forces but gave no indication of when troops might begin arriving in Zaire.
French defence officials said last week they could have 600 soldiers in place within 24 hours of U.N. approval and another 600 troops within the next 24 hours.
Defence sources have since said, however, that they did not expect French troops to begin heading for Zaire before Monday.
